name: main
prose: Entry point of ipmon, which logs IPFilter events; it returns 0 after the log reading ends, or exits. It initialises the configuration (initconfig) and parses the options (-a all logs, -b, -B binary log file, -C config file, -D daemon, -f/-I filter log, -F flush logs, -L syslog facility (an unknown name exits 1), -n resolve names, -N NAT log, -o/-O log selection, -p, -P pid file, -s syslog, -S state log, -t, -v, -x, -X); an unknown option, -h or -? calls usage(argv[0]). With -s it opens syslog with the program name and facility, initialises the tables, loads the configuration file if one was given (a load_config failure unloads it and exits 1), and defaults the first log source to the IPFilter log (the test of the three source types at lines 1652-1654 repeats logsrc[0] and so does not look at the other two). It calls openlogs, which can exit 1 when a log device cannot be opened or examined. Without -s it opens the output file argv[optind] for append (or uses stdout), exiting 1 if the open fails, and sets it unbuffered; with -s the log pointer is NULL. If -D was given and the output is not stdout, or syslog is used, it calls daemon(0, !syslog) on BSD (the result is not checked) or forks (exit 1 if fork fails, the parent exits 0) elsewhere, closes descriptors 0 and 1 and writes the pid file. It installs handlehup for SIGHUP, calls read_loginfo(&config) until it returns 0, unloads the configuration and returns 0.

name: text_open
prose: Opens the text packet-input source fname for the ipf test reader, using the module's static tfd (descriptor) and tfp (FILE pointer); it returns tfd. If tfp is non-NULL and tfd is not -1 it rewinds tfp and returns tfd without opening anything. Otherwise, for the name "-" it sets tfd to 0 and tfp to stdin; for any other name it opens fname read-only into tfd and, if that succeeded, sets tfp to fdopen(tfd, "r") (which may be NULL if fdopen fails, while tfd keeps the opened descriptor). If the open fails tfd is -1 and tfp is left as it was (it may still hold an earlier stream). It returns tfd (the descriptor, or -1).
note: ipft_tx.c:82-98 read in full. Reviewers: round 1 (on open failure tfp is not set to NULL and may retain a previous stream) right, 93-95; round 15 (fdopen failure sets tfp to NULL, not left unchanged) right, 95.

name: parseline
prose: Parses one line of the ipf text packet input into the IP packet buffer ip (large enough for ip_t plus the larger of a TCP header and an ICMP header), setting *out to 1 for an "out" line and 0 for an "in" line and, when the line has "on interface", *ifn to a strdup'd interface name; it returns 0 on success and 1 on a parse failure. It first frees *ifn if it is non-NULL (without clearing the pointer, so on a successful line without "on" *ifn is left dangling), zeroes ip and the local TCP, ICMP and option buffers, sets the IP version, header length and TTL 63, and splits the line into up to 19 whitespace-separated tokens. It returns 1 for an empty line, for a first token that does not start with 'i' or 'o' (printing a diagnostic), and (when built with IPv6) hands "in6" and "out6" lines to parseipv6. Each of the following missing tokens returns 1 without a message: the interface name after "on", the protocol, the source and destination addresses. It reads the protocol (tcp, udp or icmp, a numeric protocol, or IP), and for tcp and udp requires a comma-separated port in both the source and destination fields (a missing one prints a diagnostic and returns 1). The addresses go through tx_hostnum. For TCP it reads optional flag letters, seq= and ack=; for ICMP an optional type and code; "opt" adds IP options through buildopts. It copies the TCP, UDP or ICMP header after the IP header, stores the total length in network byte order and returns 0.
note: ipft_tx.c:156-326, with the head 190-202 read; helper functions (tx_hostnum, tx_portnum, buildopts, parseipv6) not read. Reviewers: round 1 (missing-token failures return 1 without printing) right, 192-202, 229-230, 248-249; round 15 (success without "on" leaves the freed *ifn dangling) right, 163-164. Tally 2 right.

name: fill_ip
prose: Parses the address specification av of an ipfw rule into the ipfw_insn_ip instruction cmd; cblen is the space available in the instruction buffer counted in 32-bit words (it is passed to CHECK_LENGTH, which is not read), tstate is the table state, and the function returns nothing, reporting errors by errx. It first clears the length part of cmd->o.len. The word "any" (or an abbreviation) returns leaving the length 0; "me" sets a one-instruction length and returns; a string starting "table(" is handled by fill_table with O_IP_DST_LOOKUP. Otherwise it loops over the comma-separated entries: for each it checks the remaining space, finds a separator among "/:,{", resolves the host part with lookup_host (errx(EX_NOHOST) if unknown), and builds the mask: ":" followed by a dotted netmask (invalid gives EX_DATAERR), "/" followed by a width (0 gives a zero mask, above 32 gives EX_DATAERR), "{" (a set; mask /24 assumed) or none or "," (a /32 mask); the address is ANDed with the mask. For a "{" set it requires that it is the only entry (otherwise EX_DATAERR "address set cannot be in a list"), a mask width from 24 to 31, builds a bitmap of the listed last-octet values and ranges with checks that each lies in the range and that ranges are well formed (an unclosed set, an incomplete range, an out-of-range value, an inverted range or a double '-' is EX_DATAERR), sets opcode O_IP_DST_SET with the map length and returns. An entry with a zero mask (0.0.0.0/0, meaning any) is skipped when more entries follow and, when it is the only entry, returns with a length of 0, except that "not any" gives errx(EX_DATAERR). A single plain host with mask /32 and no other entry sets the length to one ipfw_insn_u32 and returns. Other entries add two words each; at the end a total that exceeds F_LEN_MASK gives EX_DATAERR and the length is stored as the word count plus 1.
note: slice cut the head; real function fill_ip at ipfw2.c:3453-3629, read in full; fill_table, lookup_host and CHECK_LENGTH not read. Reviewers: round 1 (EX_DATAERR for 'not any' only when it is the sole entry; otherwise the entry is skipped) right, 3603-3616; round 2 (the code does not detect an unclosed set or an incomplete range) wrong: 3567-3572 reports both; round 15 (cblen counts 32-bit words, not bytes) plausible from the use in CHECK_LENGTH with F_INSN_SIZE values but not verified. Tally 1 right 1 wrong 1 unverified.

name: main
prose: Entry point of ipfw and dnctl. In Windows/TCC builds it first calls WSAStartup and returns 1 with a message if that fails. It sets g_co.prog to the dnctl or ipfw command line depending on whether the basename of av[0] is "dnctl". If there is more than one argument and the last argument starts with '/', it treats it as a file to preprocess: it calls ipfw_readfile(ac, av) when access(R_OK) succeeds and otherwise calls err(EX_USAGE, "pathname: ...") which does not return. Otherwise it calls ipfw_main(ac, av), and if that returns non-zero it calls errx(EX_USAGE, ...) with a usage message, which does not return. In the remaining cases it returns EX_OK.

name: setup_redir_port
prose: Parses a libalias "redirect_port" argument list into the buffer buf (a nat44_cfg_redir followed by one nat44_cfg_spool per comma-separated local target) and returns the number of bytes used; *ac and *av are the remaining argument count and vector and are advanced past the consumed tokens. It stores the protocol from the first token with StrToProto. The second token is the local target: if it contains a comma it is a load-sharing (LSNAT) list, which sets laddr to INADDR_NONE, lport to ~0, one local port and remembers the list; otherwise for SCTP it must not contain ':' (errx(EX_DATAERR) if it does) and is read as an address, and for other protocols it is read with StrToAddrAndPortRange (errx on an invalid range) giving the local port and the number of local ports. The third token is the public port range, with an optional address (errx on an invalid range); for SCTP the number of local ports and lport are taken from it. An optional following token beginning with a digit is the remote address, with optional port range (invalid range gives errx), otherwise the remote address is any and the remote port range is 0 with a count of 1. It requires the local and public port counts to match and the remote port to be 0 or of equal count (errx(EX_DATAERR) otherwise). For an LSNAT list it then parses each comma-separated target into a spool entry appended to the buffer: for SCTP the target must not contain ':' and its port is the public port; for other protocols it is parsed with StrToAddrAndPortRange and must name a single port, which becomes the spool port; each entry increments spool_cnt. It returns the space used.
note: slice cut the head; real function setup_redir_port at nat.c:424-585, read in full except comments (the buffer must hold the spool entries; no size checks are made). Reviewer round 15 (for a non-SCTP LSNAT list no local port is parsed from the second token (lport = ~0); the spool ports come from each target) right as to the first part, 450-454 and 566-576; the old prose said a single parsed local port. Tally 1 right.

name: nat64clat_foreach
prose: Fetches the list of nat64clat instances from the kernel and calls the callback f(cfg, name, set) once for each entry; it returns 0 on success or an errno value. It allocates a zeroed buffer of an initial size (a list header and 16 entries) with calloc and returns ENOMEM if that fails. It then calls do_get3(IP_FW_NAT64CLAT_LIST, ...): on failure it takes the size the kernel reported back in the header, frees the buffer and, if errno is ENOMEM, repeats the whole request with the new size (the calloc of the retry can again return ENOMEM); for any other errno it returns that errno. On success, if sort is non-zero it sorts the entries with qsort and nat64name_cmp, calls f for each of the olh->count entries (stepping by objsize, ignoring the result of f), frees the buffer and returns 0.

name: firmware
prose: Implements "nvmecontrol firmware" (the name of the function is firmware, not firmware_main): it downloads and/or activates an NVMe firmware image; it returns void if arg_parse fails and otherwise ends with exit(0) or an error exit. It returns at once if arg_parse(argc, argv, f) is non-zero. It then validates the options: slot 0, or a slot above 7 (other than the NONE marker), prints a message and calls arg_help; no replace image and no activate request calls arg_help; activation without an image and without a slot calls arg_help (arg_help is not read, so it is not stated whether it returns). It opens the controller (re-opening the controller device when the given device is a namespace), reads the identify data (errx(EX_IOERR) on failure) and exits through errx(EX_UNAVAILABLE) if the controller does not support firmware commands, if an image is to be written to slot 1 and slot 1 is read-only, if the slot is greater than the number of slots the controller supports, or if activation of an existing image is requested for a slot without valid firmware. It reads the image file if one was given, prints a warning and asks "Are you sure ..." until the answer starts with "yes" (continue) or "no" (exit(EX_DATAERR)). It then downloads the image (update_firmware) when given, chooses the activate action (replace and activate, replace only, or activate an existing slot), calls activate_firmware, prints whether a reboot is required or the controller reset needed when activation was requested, closes the device and exits with status 0.

Reviewers: round 15 (read-only and valid-firmware rejection apply only to narrower cases than the old prose claimed: slot 1 only with an image, valid firmware only for activation without an image) right, 289-290 and 299-301; round 17 (arg_help is not called when the slot exceeds the controller's slot count; that is errx(EX_UNAVAILABLE)) right, 294-297. Tally 2 right.

name: main
prose: Entry point of pfctl; it parses the command line, opens the pf device and performs the requested operations in a fixed order, finishing with exit(exit_val). With fewer than two arguments it calls usage(). It reads the options (-a anchor, -d, -D macro, -e, -q, -F what, -i interface, -k and -K (at most two each, otherwise usage()), -m, -M, -n, -N, -r, -f rules file, -g, -A, -R, -o optimizer, -O, -p, -P, -s what, -S, -t table, -T command, -v, -x debug, -z, -h); a repeated -F, -o, -s, -T or -x selector calls usage(), as does an unknown option or -h. It then calls errx(1) for -N together with -r; usage() when -t and -T are not used together or when operands remain where none are allowed; defaults the load flags; and, for an anchor given with -a, calls errx(1) for an empty name, a name beginning with '_' in write mode (other than for tables), or a name too long (usage() for some read-only combinations). Unless -n (no action) is set it opens the pf device and calls err(1) if that fails; with -n an open that succeeds is closed and a failed open is ignored. It opens the netlink handle (err(1, "Failed to open netlink") if that fails), allocates a path buffer (errx(1) if calloc fails), and runs, in order: disable (-d), the show options (-s), counter clearing, the clear options (-F), state and source-node killing (-k, -K), table commands (-t with -T), optimizer options (-o), loading fingerprints and rules (-f), enable (-e) and the debug level (-x); each failing step sets exit_val to 1 and the later steps still run. It ends with exit(exit_val); it does not return.

Reviewers: round 15 (main returns exit_val) wrong: line 3640 is exit(exit_val); round 17 (a failed pf device open is not an error with -n, and a netlink failure uses err, not errx) right, 3380-3388 and 3399-3400. Tally 1 right 1 wrong.

name: print_ioctl
prose: Formats the OS fingerprint fp (a struct pf_osfp_ioctl) as text in a static 1024-byte buffer and returns a pointer to that buffer (so the result is overwritten by the next call and the function is not reentrant). The colon-separated fields are: the window size, written as "*" when PF_OSFP_WSIZE_DC is set, "S" for PF_OSFP_WSIZE_MSS, "T" for PF_OSFP_WSIZE_MTU, otherwise the number fp_wsize with a "%" prefix when PF_OSFP_WSIZE_MOD is set; the TTL; the DF flag as 1 or 0; the packet size ("*" or the number, "%"-prefixed when the modulus flag is set); the TCP options from the highest-numbered stored option down, comma-separated, as N (NOP), S (SACK), T (timestamp, followed by 0 when PF_OSFP_TS0), M (MSS, followed by "*" or the possibly "%"-prefixed number) and W (window scale, followed by "*" or the possibly "%"-prefixed number), or "." when there are none (option codes other than these produce nothing); the class, version and subtype names; and a trailing "TcpOpts <count> 0x<hex>" debug field. All appends use strlcat, so output longer than the buffer is truncated.
note: slice cut the head; real function print_ioctl at pfctl_osfp.c:999-1098, read in full. Reviewer round 17 (the window size can only be numeric, "*" or "%" form) wrong: lines 1008-1011 print "S" and "T" for the MSS and MTU window flags. Tally 1 wrong.

name: ping
prose: Main routine of ping (the function called from main is named ping(argc, argv), at ping.c:197-1004); it does not return, ending with exit(nreceived ? 0 : 2). The part read here (the end of the function) starts after the options, sockets and destination have been set up: it enlarges the receive buffer, limits the capability rights of the receive socket (CAP_RECV, CAP_EVENT) and the send socket (CAP_SEND), calling err(1, ...) if caph_rights_limit fails, prints the "PING ..." banner, installs the handler onsignal for SIGINT and SIGINFO (and SIGALRM when a timeout is set; err(EX_OSERR) if sigaction fails), sets up the msghdr for receiving, and sends the first request or the preload requests (limited to npackets) with pinger(). It then loops until SIGINT is seen: on SIGINFO it prints a summary to stderr; it waits in pselect up to the interval remaining; when the socket is readable it receives with recvmsg (errors are warned about and ignored), takes the kernel timestamp or the current time, calls pr_pack and leaves the loop when the once option or npackets has been satisfied; when the wait times out (or in flood mode) it advances a sweep if one is configured (stopping when the next size would exceed the maximum), sends another request with pinger() while fewer than npackets have been sent, and otherwise leaves the loop on the second pass after setting a final wait (twice the maximum round trip, or the wait time if nothing was received); it records the largest number of missed replies. After the loop it prints the summary and calls exit(nreceived ? 0 : 2). Many earlier exits for invalid options and socket setup errors (errx with EX_USAGE, EX_NOHOST, EX_OSERR and others) occur in the part of the function that was not read in detail.
note: the packet's name main does not exist in this region: the code is the tail of ping() at ping.c:197-1004 (slice 786-1051 also includes the start of pinger() at 1015); lines 800-1004 read, lines 197-800 only listed by their err/errx exit statements ("partly read"). Previously dropped only because the name did not match.

name: ping6
prose: Main routine of ping6 (the function called from main is named ping6(argc, argv), at ping6.c:269-1273); the part read here is the end of the function, after the options, sockets and destination have been set up. It adjusts the socket buffers (err(1, ...) if the setsockopt calls for SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF, IPV6_RECVPKTINFO and IPV6_RECVHOPLIMIT fail), limits the capability rights of the two sockets by clearing CAP_SETSOCKOPT (err(1) if caph_rights_limit fails), prints the banner, and sends the first request or the preload requests (limited to npackets) with pinger(). It installs onsignal for SIGINT and SIGINFO (and SIGALRM when a timeout is set), calling err(EX_OSERR) if sigaction fails. In the loop, until SIGINT is seen, it prints a summary to stderr on SIGINFO, waits with pselect for the remaining interval and, when the socket is readable, receives with recvmsg (an error other than EINTR gives a warning and a one-second sleep; a zero-length result checks the path MTU notification and continues; otherwise it calls pr_pack); it leaves the loop when the once option or npackets is satisfied. When the wait times out (or in flood mode) it sends the next request with pinger() while fewer than npackets have been sent, otherwise it leaves the loop on the second pass after setting a final wait, and records the largest number of missed replies. After the loop it ignores SIGINT and SIGALRM, prints the summary, frees the receive packet buffer if set, and exits with 0 if any reply was received, 2 if more requests were sent than failed to send, and EX_OSERR otherwise.

name: main
prose: Entry point of reboot, halt and nextboot (selected by getprogname()): "halt" in the name sets halting, "nextboot" selects nextboot mode and its option set, anything else is reboot. It parses the options (-a, -c, -D, -d, -e, -f, -k, -l, -n, -N, -o, -p, -q, -r); an unknown option or any remaining operand calls usage(). It exits with errx(1) when the no-shutdown file exists (unless -f or nextboot), for conflicting option combinations (-D with anything else, -d with halt, -N with -n, -c with -p, -r with other options or with -k). With -D it removes the nextboot file (a missing file is fine, an unlink failure only warns) and exits 0. Unless nextboot mode, a non-root caller gets err(1) with EPERM. With -q it calls reboot(howto) directly and calls err(1) if that returns. A -k kernel name is checked (unless -f) to be an existing regular file, then added to the next-boot environment; a non-empty environment is written to the nextboot file with write_nextboot; in nextboot mode it then exits 0. Otherwise it logs the shutdown (unless -l), records a SHUTDOWN_TIME utmpx entry, syncs unless -n or -N, and ignores SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGQUIT, SIGTERM, SIGTSTP and SIGPIPE. With -r it sends SIGEMT to init (err(1) if that fails) and returns 0, the only return of the function. Otherwise it sends SIGTSTP to init (err(1) on failure), SIGTERM to all processes (err(1) on failure other than ESRCH), waits for paging to settle, repeatedly sends SIGKILL (a failure other than ESRCH goes to the restart path, a missing process ends the loop, and after 5 rounds it warns and stops), and calls reboot(howto). The restart path calls errx(1) after trying to send SIGHUP to init; the message mentions "(can't restart init)" only if that kill fails.

Reviewer round 15 (SIGHUP is sent on SIGTERM failure) wrong: a SIGTERM failure other than ESRCH calls err(1) immediately (458-459); the SIGHUP to init is only on the restart path (496-500) reached from a SIGKILL error. Tally 1 wrong.

name: main
prose: Entry point of recoverdisk, which copies a possibly failing disk to a file or reads it, keeping a worklist of areas still to be read. It makes stdout and stderr unbuffered and parses the options -b big read size, -i interval, -l log file (opened for append, err(1) on failure), -p error pause, -m medium read size, -r read worklist file, -s small read size, -t total size, -u unreadable pattern, -v verbose, -w write worklist file; an unknown option calls usage(), as does a number of operands other than one or two. It opens the first operand read-only (err(1) on failure), determines the total size and the read sizes, allocates the work buffer (asserted), and when a second operand is given opens it for writing with O_CREAT and truncates it to the total size (err(1) on failure), otherwise write_fd is -1. If an unreadable pattern is given it prepares a pattern buffer. It loads the worklist from -r (the done size is the total minus the remaining work) or starts with one lump covering the whole device. If -w was given it installs sighandler for SIGINT. It then loops while aborting is not set: it sleeps for the interval, calls attempt_one_lump, ends when that returns 0 (no more work), counts successful reads and saves the worklist every snapshot period (60 seconds), reports progress, and on a failed read (negative result) adjusts the read sizes and stops with aborting set when errno is EINVAL or ENXIO; otherwise it reports and continues. The loop also ends when SIGINT sets aborting through sighandler (when -w was given). After the loop it saves the worklist, frees the buffers, reports and returns 0 (the return value is marked XXX in the source), so a read error does not change the exit status.

name: setdirmodes
prose: Applies the owner, mode, extended attributes, times and flags recorded in the mode file to the directories restored by restore; flags may contain FORCE. The mode file name modefile is rebuilt from TMPDIR (or _PATH_TMP) and dumpdate when the command is 'r' or 'R'. If modefile starts with '#' it calls panic("modefile not defined") (which terminates the program; the lines after it are unreachable). If fopen fails it prints a diagnostic and returns. It then reads struct modeinfo records until end of file or a read error (a warning and a break); for a record with an extended attribute block it reads it into a malloc'd buffer (if malloc fails the block is skipped with fseek). For each record it looks up the entry by inode number. For the 'i' and 'x' commands: an unknown inode is skipped; an entry that already existed (EXISTED) is skipped, after clearing its NEW flag, unless FORCE is set; and for the root inode it asks reply("set owner/mode for '.'") and skips the entry if the answer is FAIL. For other commands an unknown inode calls panic (terminating). Unless Nflag is set it then chowns (a non-root caller uses its own uid with the recorded gid), chmods, sets extended attributes when present and the buffer was obtained, sets the times with utimensat and the flags with chflags, ignoring their errors. It clears the entry's NEW flag in every non-skipped case, including when Nflag is set. At the end it frees the buffer and closes the file.
note: slice cut the head; real function setdirmodes at dirs.c:552-663, read in full; panic, reply, set_extattr not read. Reviewers: original (EXISTED without FORCE and a FAIL reply skip the entry) right, 626-632; round 2 (the panic on '#' terminates so the function does not return as stated) right, 568-572; round 15 (the NEW flag is cleared regardless of Nflag) right, 658. Tally 3 right.

name: findinode
prose: Reads tape headers from the dump until a header that describes a file, and fills in the global curfile from it; header is the current header and dumpdate the dump date being restored. It first resets curfile to the name "<name unknown>", action UNKNOWN, mode 0 and ino 0. Then it loops, switching on the header type: for TS_ADDR it skips the data blocks the header lists (reading them with readtape) and reads headers with gethead until one succeeds with the right dump date (counting skipped blocks, with Dflag byte-slide bookkeeping), and the loop repeats; for TS_INODE it copies the mode, owner, flags, rdev, times, size and the inode number from the header into curfile and ends the loop; for TS_END, if tapesread & (tapesread + 1) is non-zero it calls getvol(0) and continues, which re-tests the loop condition and, because the type is not TS_ADDR, ends the loop with curfile.ino still 0, otherwise it sets curfile.ino to maxino and ends; TS_CLRI and TS_BITS set the name to "<file removal list>" or "<file dump list>" (ino stays 0); for TS_TAPE and unknown types it either prints a message (with Dflag) and skips headers with gethead until a good one, or calls panic (terminating) without Dflag. The loop repeats only while the header type is TS_ADDR (while (htype == TS_ADDR)); afterwards, if any blocks were skipped it prints a "resync restore, skipped N bytes/blocks" message and resets the skip count.
note: slice cut the head; real function findinode at tape.c:1460-1567, read in full to 1567. Reviewers: original (TS_TAPE and the default path skip or panic without populating curfile from that header) right, 1530-1553; round 15 (TS_END with tapesread & (tapesread + 1) calls getvol and continues without setting ino = maxino) right, 1513-1519. Tally 2 right.

name: input
prose: Handles one received RIP packet in routed: input(from, sifp, aifp, rip, cc) returns nothing; the part read here is the RIP_RESPONSE case, ending in the loop that processes the route entries (n points at the first entry and lim at the end). The whole response is discarded with a rate-limited message (and the function returns) when the source port is not the RIP port, when rip_sock is closed, when the sender is one of this host's own addresses on a non-remote interface, when no receiving interface can be found (aifp NULL), when the interface has RIP input off, when the response is empty (n >= lim), when the interface rejects that RIP version (IS_NO_RIPV1_IN or IS_NO_RIPV2_IN), when the interface is marked broken, when it is IS_DISTRUST and the sender is not in the trusted-gateway list, or when authentication is configured, the packet is not RIPv1 and ck_passwd fails. Otherwise it loops over the entries: authentication entries are skipped; an entry of an unsupported address family is skipped with a message; an invalid destination (check_dst) or a metric of 0 or above HOPCNT_INFINITY discards the rest of the packet (return); a next hop is honoured only for RIPv2 on the interface's network, else cleared; the mask is derived (RIPv1 or a zero mask uses the classful mask, a mask inconsistent with the destination skips the entry); the metric is increased by the interface metric and the inbound adjustment, capped at HOPCNT_INFINITY; entries from a trusted gateway outside its allowed nets, and default routes whose metric reaches the interface's default threshold, are skipped; for RIPv1 hosts it may expand a classful route into several subnet routes (not more than 510) and then calls input_route for each destination of the expansion with the new route record (gate, router, metric, tag, time, interface). The function returns void after the loop. The code before line 511 (other commands, the request case) was not read ("partly read").
note: the named function rip_input does not exist; the slice is the tail of input() at input.c:125-768, with lines 500-768 read in full and lines 125-500 not read. Previously dropped only because the name did not match.

name: set_rdisc_mg
prose: Joins or leaves the ICMP router discovery multicast groups on the interface ifp (assert ifp != NULL); on non-zero joins as appropriate and on zero leaves; it returns nothing and logs socket errors with LOGERR. If rdisc_sock is not open: it returns if on is zero or the interface has IS_NO_RDISC set, and otherwise opens the socket. If the interface lacks IFF_MULTICAST it clears IS_ALL_HOSTS and IS_ALL_ROUTERS in ifp->int_state and returns. For the all-hosts group: if this host is a supplier, the interface has IS_NO_ADV_IN, or on is zero, it leaves the group when IS_ALL_HOSTS is set (a failing MCAST_LEAVE_GROUP is only logged) and clears IS_ALL_HOSTS in every case, even if the leave failed; otherwise, if IS_ALL_HOSTS is not set, it joins the group and sets IS_ALL_HOSTS only when the join succeeded. For the all-routers group: if this host is not a supplier, the interface has IS_NO_ADV_OUT, or on is zero, it leaves the group when IS_ALL_ROUTERS is set and clears the bit (even if the leave failed); otherwise, if the bit is not set, it joins and sets IS_ALL_ROUTERS on success only.

Reviewers: original (the bits are cleared even when MCAST_LEAVE_GROUP fails, so they need not reflect real membership) right, 196-202 and 222-228; round 15 (ALL_ROUTERS leave/join conditions are inverted relative to the old prose) right: the code leaves when not supplier and joins when supplier (217-231). Tally 2 right.

name: rdisc_age
prose: Ages the table of discovered routers drs[] and re-selects the preferred one; bad_gate is 0 or the address of a gateway that has stopped working; it returns nothing. If this host is a supplier it calls rdisc_sort() when a discovered route is currently in use (cur_drp non-NULL; rdisc_sort may itself remove expired entries), then rdisc_adv() to send advertisements, and returns without any aging or bad-gateway handling. Otherwise, if bad_gate is non-zero, it finds the entry for that gateway and, if its timestamp is later than the value that would make it expire one supply interval from now, moves its timestamp back to that value (so it expires sooner). It then calls rdisc_sol() to send solicitations and rdisc_sort() to age and select, and when the RIP socket is closed and bad_gate is 0 it calls age(0).

Reviewers: original (in supplier mode it returns early without aging expired or bad-gateway routes) right, 299-306; round 15 (in supplier mode rdisc_sort may delete expired discovered routers, so "without deleting anything" is wrong) plausible but rdisc_sort was not read, so only stated as possible. Tally 1 right 1 unverified.

name: DoFile
prose: Processes one dump device for savecore: it examines the kernel dump header at the end of the device and, depending on the options, checks for a dump, saves it (possibly compressed, uncompressed or decrypted) into savedir and records it with info and symlinks, and clears the dump header unless keep is set; it returns nothing. It returns early (after a message) when a live core is requested, when the XML output stream cannot be created, when the work buffer cannot be allocated, or when the device cannot be opened. It reads the device size and the last header (a short sector, a failed allocation or seek or read goes to the cleanup that closes the descriptor), and decides from the header magic whether it is a text or regular kernel dump, a cleared header or garbage, checking the version and the header parity; a bad version, parity or non-matching first and last headers makes it stop (go to cleanup) unless force is set, and a cleared or unknown magic stops it unless forced. With -c (clear) it goes to the header-clearing step; with the check option (checkfor) it exits with EXIT_SUCCESS when a valid dump is present. Otherwise it computes the dump length, checks that the save directory has enough space (stop if not), opens the core file (and a compressing stream when compress is set), writes the info file, for an encrypted dump reads the key (stop on failure), and copies the data with DoTextdumpFile or DoRegularFile (a failure goes to the cleanup that closes everything); it closes the core file, creates the info.last, key.last and core.last symlinks (failures are logged), and, unless keep is set, overwrites the dump header on the device to mark it cleared. It finishes the XML output and returns; the cleanup paths close the files and the device.

name: main
prose: Entry point of tunefs, which changes tunable parameters in a UFS superblock; it does not return. With fewer than 3 arguments it calls usage(). It parses the options (-A, -a, -e, -f, -j, -J, -k, -L, -l, -m, -N, -n, -o, -p, -s, -S, -t), counting each in found_arg and validating its value with errx(10, ...) on a bad value (for example enable/disable values, numbers below their minimum, an over-long or invalid volume label, -m outside 0 to 99, -o other than space or time); an unknown option calls usage(). It calls usage() if no option was given or the operand count is not one. It opens the disk with ufs_disk_fillout and reads the superblock (a failure goes to the error exit). If the filesystem is not clean (or has a needs-fsck flag) and more than one option was given or -p is not the only option, it calls errx(1, "... not clean - run fsck"). With -p it prints the current tuning values and exits 0. Otherwise it applies each requested change in turn to the in-memory superblock, printing whether the value changed or stayed the same (some changes can fail with a message, for example enabling journaling on a filesystem that cannot take it). It then writes the superblock with sbwrite; a failure goes to the error exit, which calls errx(11) when the disk has an error message and err(12) otherwise. On success it closes the disk, calls chkdoreload for the mount point and exits 0.
note: slice cut the head; real main at tunefs.c:~94-572 (the head near line 89-95 and the option loop read; the long per-option change bodies 314-540 only skimmed, partly read). Reviewers: round 15 (the unclean check uses found_arg, not the number of changes; -p plus one change exits 1) right, 306-309; round 17 (a superblock write failure exits via err(13), not errx(11)/err(12)) wrong: the error exit at the end of main uses errx(11) or err(12), lines 566-571. Tally 1 right 1 wrong.

name: readfd
prose: Handles readability of the health-check connection of l4 (an l4cfg_t with descriptor l4_fd). If l4_rw is -2 (the connection is still being established) it calls connectfd(l4) and returns without reading. Otherwise it receives with recv: into the rest of l4_rbuf (l4_rsize - l4_rlen bytes at offset l4_rlen) when a response size is configured, else into a local 80-byte buffer. A recv result of 0 or -1 calls closel4(l4, 1), which closes the socket and (per its argument) removes the NAT rule if the target was alive. For a positive result: with no configured response size (local buffer) the data is NUL-terminated and, if the target was not alive, it is marked alive, addnat(l4) is called and closel4(l4, 0) closes the connection; with a configured response size the received count is added to l4_rlen and, once l4_rlen reaches l4_rsize, the buffer is compared with the expected response: a match marks the target alive and calls addnat if it was not alive already, then closes with closel4(l4, 0); a mismatch calls closel4(l4, 1). Until the whole response has arrived the function returns without closing.
note: readfd at l4check.c:208-268, read in full; closel4 at 142-151 read (it closes the socket, and with dead set and the target alive marks it dead and calls delnat). Reviewers: original (l4_rlen grows only when l4_rsize is non-zero; the l4_rw == -2 path was omitted) right, 215-218 and 243-244; round 15 (the mismatch path removes the NAT rule only when l4_alive, not always) right, 147-150. Tally 2 right.

name: parse_req
prose: Parses the first tokens of a control-transfer command line into the global libusb20 setup packet (bmRequestType, bRequest, wValue, wIndex, wLength); argv holds argc tokens. It examines at most seven tokens (idx 0 to 6) and stops early when no tokens remain. Token 0 selects the direction by its first letter: 'i' sets bit 0x80, 'o' leaves it clear, anything else prints a message and returns -1. Token 1 selects the type by its first letter: 's' standard, 'c' class (0x20), 'v' vendor (0x40), otherwise a message and return -1. Token 2 selects the recipient by its first letter: 'd' device, 'i' interface (1), 'e' endpoint (2), 'o' other (3), otherwise a message and return -1; after a valid recipient it stores the accumulated request type in setup.bmRequestType. Token 3 is converted to bRequest with get_req (not read), and tokens 4, 5 and 6 are converted with strtoul (base detected) into wValue, wIndex and wLength. Fields for tokens that are not present are not touched, and bmRequestType is only stored when token 2 is reached. On success it returns the value of argc after the loop, which is the number of tokens left unconsumed (0 when seven or fewer tokens were given), and -1 on any invalid direction, type or recipient.
note: slice cut the head; real function parse_req at control.c:224-301, read in full; get_req not read. Reviewers: round 1 (not all setup fields are filled when fewer than six tokens are given) right, 229 and 280; the old prose also said the function examines at most seven tokens, which matches. The return value (remaining token count rather than a success flag) was not stated before.

name: command_bcache
prose: Boot-loader command handler for "bcachestat"; argc and argv come from the command interpreter and argv is unused. If argc != 1 it sets command_errmsg to "wrong number of arguments" and returns CMD_ERROR without printing. Otherwise it prints the block cache statistics (total blocks, block size, read-ahead, unit blocks, cached units, operations, bypasses, hits and misses, from the bcache globals) and returns CMD_OK.
note: slice cut the head; real function command_bcache at bcache.c:506-521 (registered by COMMAND_SET at 503), read in full. Reviewer round 17 (the formal contract omits command_errmsg and the printing side effects) right; contract removed. Tally 1 right.

name: autoboot
prose: Counts down and then boots the default kernel, or returns to the loader prompt when interrupted; it sets autoboot_tried to 1 first and returns a CMD_* code. A timeout of -1 means use the "autoboot_delay" environment variable in seconds (10 if unset or unparseable). If the "kernelname" variable is unset it calls loadakernel(0, 0, argv) and, if it is still unset, sets command_errmsg to "no valid kernel found" and returns CMD_ERROR. If the timeout is negative it boots at once; otherwise it prints a prompt (the custom one or the default) and waits for the deadline: it polls the console; in the default build an Enter key sets yes and any other key leaves the loop with yes still 0 (no boot); when the BOOT_PROMPT_123 option is compiled in, Enter boots, and the sequence "1", "2", "3" leaves the loop with yes = 0 (any wrong key restarts the sequence); when the deadline passes yes is set to 1. It prints a countdown once per second. If yes is set it prints the "Booting" message and returns the result of command_boot with "boot"; otherwise it returns CMD_OK after a newline, which hands control to the command prompt.
note: slice cut the head; real function autoboot at boot.c:172-262, read in full (command_autoboot at 130-155 only calls it). Reviewers: original (omits the non-boot return CMD_OK when the countdown is interrupted) right, 261; round 15 (the "123" sequence breaks with yes = 0, leading to the command prompt, not command_boot) right, 226-229. Tally 2 right.

name: gfx_get_ppi
prose: Returns the pixels-per-inch estimate of the framebuffer: it calls edid_diagonal_squared() and returns 0 if that is 0 (no usable EDID size, so no division by zero happens); otherwise it computes dp = fb_width squared plus fb_height squared (in unsigned arithmetic) from the global gfx_state and returns isqrt(dp / di). It acquires nothing.
note: gfx_get_ppi at gfx_fb.c:2113-2127, read in full. Reviewer round 1 (the early return of 0 prevents a division by zero) right, 2117-2119; the old prose already described it.

name: gfx_get_font
prose: Chooses a font from the global font list for a terminal of rows by cols characters on a screen of height by width pixels; it returns the font bitmap data or NULL. It returns NULL for a text framebuffer (FB_TEXT) and when gfx_get_ppi() is 0. It computes a target font height from the screen's pixels per inch. It then walks the font list (sorted by size): it skips fonts that would not fit rows and cols on the screen; for the first font that fits and where the next font in the list is missing or smaller than the target height it uses it, loading it with its font_load callback if its bitmap is not loaded or it is flagged FONT_RELOAD (the result of font_load, which can be NULL, becomes the returned value), and stops; fonts that fit but are not selected make the candidate NULL again. It returns the candidate (NULL if none was chosen).
note: gfx_get_font at gfx_fb.c:2139-2190, read in full. Previously unreviewed; the old prose is consistent but did not say that the result is the callback's return value.

name: set_font
prose: Selects the font for a screen of h by w pixels and updates *rows and *cols to the character grid that fits; it returns font bitmap data (never NULL when the default font data is available). It first looks for a font flagged FONT_MANUAL, loading it if needed (a font whose bitmap is still NULL is discarded); if none, it asks gfx_get_font for the best match. When a font is found it sets *rows = h / font height and *cols = w / font width and returns it. Otherwise it scans the font list for the first font that fits the existing rows and cols (or the default font on very large screens), loading it when needed (a failed load skips the font), and on success updates *rows and *cols from it and stops. If still nothing was chosen it tries to load the last font in the list and, failing that, uses the built-in default font; in this case it also updates *rows and *cols from the font and returns it.
note: set_font at gfx_fb.c:2193-2272, read in full. The old prose said it always returns non-NULL; the code returns the address of the default font data as the final fallback, so NULL is returned only if that address were NULL (it is not).

name: cons_clear
prose: Clears the framebuffer console: it feeds the two-byte reset sequence ESC 'c' to the teken emulator with teken_input(&gfx_state.tg_teken, clear, 2) and then calls gfx_state.tg_functions->tf_param(&gfx_state, TP_SHOWCURSOR, 0) to hide the cursor. It returns nothing and acquires nothing.
note: cons_clear at gfx_fb.c:2275-2282, read in full.

name: setup_font
prose: Chooses a font and applies it to the teken graphics state; it returns nothing. It calls set_font(&state->tg_tp.tp_row, &state->tg_tp.tp_col, height, width), which updates the row and column counts, and calls panic("out of memory") if set_font returns NULL. It then copies the font maps and map counts (VFNT_MAPS of them) from the chosen font into state->tg_font, copies the byte count, height and width, and sets the environment variable "screen.font" to "<width>x<height>" (volatile, no hook, with font_set as the set hook and env_nounset as the unset hook).
note: setup_font at gfx_fb.c:2285-2316, read in full except the middle of the map copy loop details.

name: efi_term_emu
prose: Processes one output character c for the EFI console, emulating a subset of ANSI/cons25 escape sequences when TERM_EMU is defined; it returns nothing. It returns immediately, doing nothing, if boot_services_active is false. When TERM_EMU is not defined it passes c to efi_cons_rawputchar and returns. When it is defined the function is a state machine on the static esc, args and argc: in the normal state (esc 0) an ESC byte only records the state and any other byte goes to efi_cons_rawputchar; after ESC a '[' starts a numeric-argument sequence (args[0] cleared, argc -1) and any other byte calls bail_out(c); within "ESC [" a ';' advances to the next argument (bail_out when there would be more than MAXARGS), 'H' calls HO() with no argument or CM() with exactly one extra argument (otherwise bail_out), 'J' with no argument calls CD() (otherwise bail_out), 'm' applies the colour and attribute arguments to the global foreground and background (0 reset, 1 bold, 4 and 5 bright background, 7 reverse, 22, 24, 25, 30-37, 39, 40-47 and 49) and calls SetAttribute on the console output and end_term(), a digit is accumulated with get_arg, and any other byte calls bail_out(c); any unknown esc state calls bail_out(c). The helpers HO, CM, CD, bail_out, end_term and get_arg were not read, so the memory and console effects of CD (which may allocate and free) are not described here.
note: efi_term_emu at efi_console.c:748-870, read in full; the macros/functions it calls were not read ("partly read"). Reviewers: original (without TERM_EMU the function does nothing; the annotation claims processing and omits the 'm' handler) wrong for the #else branch at 867-868 (it calls efi_cons_rawputchar) but right that the old prose omitted 'm'; round 15 (CD/CL may malloc and free memory) not checked. Tally 1 mixed 1 unchecked.

name: efi_redirect_exceptions
prose: Installs the loader's own IDT (and, if needed, GDT and TSS) so that CPU exceptions raised while UEFI boot services are active are handled by the loader's handlers, returning 1 on success and 0 on failure (in every failure case after the first allocation it calls free_tables() to release what was set up). It saves the firmware IDT with sidt and allocates pages for the loader IDT (AllocatePages; on failure it prints a message, clears lidt_pa and returns 0) and one page for an exception stack (failure: message, free_tables(), return 0), then copies the firmware IDT contents into the loader IDT. It saves the firmware GDT and task register. If the firmware has no TSS loaded (task register 0) it looks for a free system-segment slot in the firmware GDT; if none, it checks that the table can grow (message, free_tables() and return 0 if all 8190 slots are used), allocates and fills a larger GDT (failure: message, free_tables(), return 0), and sets up a new TSS with efi_setup_tss (failure: free_tables(), return 0); if the firmware has a TSS it validates its descriptor type (a non-TSS descriptor gives a message, free_tables() and return 0) and marks it not busy. It prepares the handlers for the exception vectors 0 to 14 and 16 to 20, chooses an unused IST index (all used: message, free_tables(), clear lidt_pa, return 0), sets that IST in each intercepted IDT entry and stores the exception stack top in the TSS. With interrupts disabled it loads the new GDT (if one was made), the new TSS and the loader IDT, restores the interrupt state and returns 1.
note: slice cut the head; real function efi_redirect_exceptions at trap.c:239-390, read in full; efi_setup_tss, free_tables and the PREPARE_EXCEPTION macro not read. Reviewer round 1 (formal contract only ensures the return value) right, contract removed.

name: fdt_fixup_stdout
prose: If the /chosen node of the loaded device tree has no "stdout" property, sets "stdout" and "stdin" to the path of a matching serial node derived from the console name str; it returns nothing. It sets ptr to the last character of str and then runs a loop that decrements str while ptr > str and the byte before str is a digit (the test reads *(str - 1), i.e. memory before the start of the string, and str moves backwards, not the tail of the name; with a typical name where that byte is not a digit the loop does not run). It returns without changes when ptr == str (which holds for a one-character string whose preceding byte is not a digit), when /chosen cannot be found, or when "stdout" already exists with non-zero length. Otherwise it builds the string "serial" followed by up to three characters copied from ptr (the last character of the original name, for a name like "uart0" giving "serial0"), returns without changes if strlen(ptr) > 3, looks the path up with fdt_path_offset (return if it is not found) and sets both "stdout" and "stdin" in /chosen to that string.
note: slice cut the head; real function fdt_fixup_stdout at fdt_loader_cmd.c:888-931, read in full. Reviewers: original (the digit loop tests *(str - 1), not ptr, so it uses the last character rather than a numeric tail) right, 895-897 and 917; round 2 (an empty string does not leave the tree unchanged) right: strlen(str) - 1 for an empty string gives ptr one before the string (895); round 15 (precondition issue about reading before the string) right, 896. Tally 3 right.

name: ficlNtohl
prose: Returns ntohl(number): the low 32 bits of number are converted from network (big-endian) byte order to host byte order and the result is returned zero-extended as an unsigned long. On a little-endian host this swaps the four low bytes; on a big-endian host it returns the low 32 bits unchanged. The upper bits of number are ignored. It has no side effects.
note: unix.c:6-9 read in full. The previous contract assumed a byte swap on every host, which is only right for little-endian targets; contract removed.

name: ofCoIm
prose: Compile-time (immediate) word for OF in a FICL CASE ... OF ... ENDOF construct; vm is the FICL virtual machine and the function returns nothing. It asserts that pSys->pBranch0 is set. If the top of the parameter stack is the fallthroughTag (left by a preceding fallthrough), it checks it with matchControlTag and pops its fixup pointer; then it requires a caseTag control frame to follow (matchControlTag) and re-marks it with markControlTag. It then appends the OF-paren runtime cell (pSys->pOfParen) to the dictionary, pushes an ofTag branch fixup with markBranch, and appends a single cell holding the value 2 (dictAppendUNS(dp, 2), one cell). If there was a fallthrough fixup it patches that earlier branch with the distance from it to the current dictionary position (here). The caseTag is expected below the fallthroughTag when both are present, not on top.
note: ofCoIm at words.c:1444-1476, read in full; matchControlTag, markControlTag and markBranch not read. Reviewers: original (the placeholder is a single cell holding 2, not two cells) right, 1467; round 15 (the fallthroughTag is on top when present, with the caseTag below it) right, 1455-1461. Tally 2 right.

name: parse_cmds
prose: Parses the boot command string cmdstr (modified in place: a NUL replaces the separator after each token) and applies option switches, a disk specification and a kernel name; dskupdated is set to 0 on entry and to 1 when a "disk(...)" specification was parsed. Tokens are separated by blanks, tabs and newlines. A token starting with '-' is a list of option letters: 'P' prints the keyboard status (and, when no keyboard is present, sets the dual-console and serial flags), 'S' followed by decimal digits that end the token sets comspeed when the number is positive and ends that token's scan, and any other letter must be one of the letters in optstr, whose flag in opts is toggled (an unknown letter returns -1). After the letters ioctrl is recomputed from the dual and serial flags and, if serial is used, sio_init is called with 115200 / comspeed (on failure the serial bit is dropped). Any other token is a kernel name, optionally preceded by a disk specification "[drive:]xx(unit p part)": a malformed specification (drive digit above 9, name length not 2, an unknown device name, unit above 9 or missing 'p', partition outside 1 to 128, missing ')') returns -1; a valid one sets gdsk.dsk type, unit, part and drive and dskupdated to 1. A remaining name longer than or equal to sizeof(kname) returns -1, otherwise it is copied to kname. The function returns 0 when all tokens are consumed and -1 on the first invalid token.
note: slice cut the head; real function parse_cmds at gptboot.c:498-598 (the name parse does not exist), read in full. The old prose omitted the return -1 cases.

name: parse_cmd
prose: Parses the global boot command string cmd (no parameters; the string is modified in place) in the ZFS boot loader, applying option switches, listing, a status request, a root dataset and a kernel name; it returns 0 when all tokens were consumed and -1 on a problem or after an informational command. Tokens are separated by blanks, tabs and newlines. A token starting with '-' is a list of option letters: 'P' prints the keyboard status (and sets the dual and serial flags when there is no keyboard), 'S' followed by a positive number that ends the token sets comspeed, any other letter must be in optstr (otherwise -1) and toggles its flag in opts; then ioctrl is recomputed and sio_init(115200 / comspeed) is called when serial is used (failure drops the serial bit). Because the following test is written "} if (c == '?')" rather than "else if", after processing a '-' token control falls on to the final else branch with the rest of the token as if it were a name, so the next steps also run for such tokens. A token starting with '?' lists the files and ZFS datasets at the given path (default "/") and returns -1. Otherwise the token "status" prints the status of all devices through the pager and returns -1; a token that may start with "zfs:" and contain ':' is passed to mount_root (return -1 if that fails) and the part after it is the kernel name; a remaining name of sizeof(kname) or more returns -1, otherwise it is copied to kname.
note: slice cut the head; the real function parse_cmd at zfsboot.c:563-677, read in full; mount_root, fs_list, zfs_list not read. The old prose had a different shape (it did not note the missing else at line 616); reviewer round 1 (formal contract only ensures the result) right, contract removed.

name: biospnp_call
prose: Calls a PnP BIOS function through the real-mode BIOS entry point and returns the low 16 bits of the BIOS's eax result (the PnP status code). The function number func is packed first as a 16-bit value into a local array of four 32-bit words that starts zeroed, then each variadic argument is packed according to fmt: a 'w' takes a u_int argument stored as 16 bits, an 'l' takes a uint32_t stored as 32 bits, and other format characters are ignored; the BIOS data segment pnp_Icheck->pnp_rmds is appended last as 16 bits (the caller must not pass more than the four words allow; there is no bounds check). It sets the v86 control to a far call to the BIOS entry address (pnp_rmcs:pnp_rmip from pnp_Icheck), runs v86bios with the four packed words as stack arguments and returns v86.eax & 0xffff.
note: slice cut the head; real function biospnp_call at biospnp.c:248-296, read in full; v86bios not read. Previously dropped only because the name was not in the slice.

name: spinc_putchar
prose: Output routine of the spinning-cursor console: the character argument c is ignored; instead it draws the next frame of a spinner on the parent console, at most once per second. It reads the current time; if now is less than lasttime + 1 it returns without output or state change. Otherwise, when TERM_EMU is defined and lasttime is non-zero, it first writes a backspace '\b' to the parent; then it sets lasttime to now, writes the low byte of the static tw_chars (initially '|' from the value 0x5C2D2F7C) to the parent with c_out, and rotates tw_chars right by one byte (so the successive characters are '|', '/', '-', '\' and then repeat). The low-byte extraction does not depend on the host byte order because it is a numeric cast. parent must be non-NULL (set by spinc_probe).
note: spinc_putchar at spinconsole.c:78-94, read in full. Reviewers: original (omits the TERM_EMU backspace side effect) right, 87-90; round 15 (the emitted sequence is not endian-dependent: the cast takes the low byte, always '|' first) right, 92.

name: device_probe_and_attach
prose: Tries to find and attach a driver module for the device dev (whose parent must be set) in the kernel-shim bus framework; it returns 0 on success and ENODEV otherwise. It returns 0 immediately if the device is already attached. Otherwise, for each registered module whose bus_name equals the parent's name, it finds the module's device class; if the device is not already in that class it skips the module when the device has a fixed class, removes the device from its old class and adds it to the new one (skipping the module if the add fails); it then records the module in dev->dev_module and, if DEVICE_PROBE(dev) returns 0 or less, calls device_allocate_softc (a zero-size softc is allowed, in which case nothing is allocated and it still returns 0) and, if that returns 0, DEVICE_ATTACH; when attach succeeds it sets dev_attached to 1 and returns 0. In every other case (probe returned positive, softc allocation failed, or attach failed) it calls device_detach(dev) and tries the next module. After all modules have been tried without success it returns ENODEV, which is therefore also the result when modules matched but failed to probe or attach.
note: device_probe_and_attach at bsd_kernel.c:926-975, read in full; device_allocate_softc, devclass_* and device_detach not read. Reviewers: original (ENODEV is also returned when matching modules fail probe or attach) right, 971-974; round 15 (success can occur with a zero-size driver without allocating a softc) plausible from the comment in the old prose but device_allocate_softc was not read, so stated hedged.
